question: What is JSON and why is it the dominant data format for REST APIs?
title: JSON in REST APIs
direct_answer: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text-based data format using key-value pairs, arrays, and nested objects. REST APIs use JSON because it's human-readable, language-agnostic, natively supported by browsers, and more compact than XML.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of JSON structure and why REST adopted it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing JSON data types or thinking JSON is JavaScript-only
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention JSON's limitations (no comments, no date type) and how Spring handles them

sections.title: Why JSON Won
sections.content: JSON replaced XML in REST APIs because it's simpler, more compact, and native to JavaScript. A 100-byte JSON payload might need 200+ bytes as XML with all its tags. Every modern language has JSON libraries. Browsers parse JSON natively with JSON.parse(). Spring Boot uses Jackson library to automatically serialize/deserialize JSON.

sections.title: JSON Structure and Data Types
content: Data types: string ("name"), number (42, 3.14), boolean (true/false), null, object {}, array []
No date type — dates are strings: ISO 8601 format '2025-01-15T10:30:00Z'
No comments allowed in JSON
JSON vs XML: JSON is ~30% smaller, easier to read, no namespaces
Jackson annotations: @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonFormat
Content-Type: application/json in HTTP headers

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation but it's language-agnostic. REST APIs use JSON because it's compact, human-readable, and every programming language can parse it. It supports six data types: strings, numbers, booleans, null, objects, and arrays. One important thing to know is that JSON has no native date type — we send dates as strings, typically in ISO 8601 format like 2025-01-15. In Spring Boot, Jackson handles all the serialization automatically. You just return your Java objects and Jackson converts them to JSON.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: JSON won the API data format wars for one reason — it's simple enough to read as a human and parse as a machine in every language.

beats.text: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a lightweight text format for structured data. Despite the name it's language-agnostic — every modern language has a JSON library. A JSON document is made of key-value pairs inside curly braces (objects) or values inside square brackets (arrays), and the values can be nested indefinitely.

REST APIs chose JSON over XML because JSON is 20-30% smaller for the same data, has no angle-bracket noise, and browsers parse it natively. Every mobile and web client works with JSON without extra libraries.

items: Six data types: string (quoted), number (unquoted), boolean (true/false), null, object {}, array []
No native date type — dates travel as ISO 8601 strings like 2026-06-02T10:30:00Z
No comments allowed in JSON — it's pure data, no annotation
Content-Type header: application/json — both request and response should declare this

beats.text: Todo API response: GET /todos/42 returns {id:42, title:Buy milk, done:false, createdAt:2026-06-01T08:00:00Z}. The id and done fields are number and boolean. The createdAt is a string — there's no date type in JSON itself. Spring Boot uses Jackson to turn the Java LocalDateTime into that ISO string automatically. POST /todos expects the same shape (minus id, which the server assigns). candidates miss: many candidates say JSON is JavaScript-specific. It's not. The name is historical. Python, Java, Go, Ruby all parse and produce JSON natively.

items: Saying JSON is JavaScript-only — the name is historical; it's a universal text format supported by every language
Sending dates as milliseconds or custom strings — use ISO 8601 (2026-06-01T10:00:00Z) so every client parses correctly

speakable_v2.cap: JSON = key-value text format, six types, no dates, no comments. Language-agnostic. Spring Boot's Jackson turns Java objects to JSON and back automatically.

question: How does Spring Boot serialize and deserialize JSON with Jackson?
title: Jackson JSON Serialization in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson as the default JSON processor. @RestController methods returning objects are automatically serialized to JSON. @RequestBody deserializes incoming JSON to Java objects. Jackson annotations customize the behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of how Spring Boot handles JSON under the hood
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about Jackson's default behavior like ignoring unknown properties
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show knowledge of @JsonProperty, @JsonIgnore, @JsonFormat, and ObjectMapper configuration

sections.title: Jackson in Spring Boot
sections.content: Spring Boot includes Jackson in spring-boot-starter-web. When you annotate a class with @RestController and return a Java object, Spring automatically calls Jackson's ObjectMapper to convert it to JSON. For incoming requests with @RequestBody, Jackson deserializes the JSON body to your Java object.

sections.title: Key Jackson Annotations
content: @JsonProperty("user_name") — map Java field to different JSON key
@JsonIgnore — exclude field from serialization/deserialization
@JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd") — format dates
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL) — skip null fields
@JsonNaming(SnakeCaseStrategy.class) — convert camelCase to snake_case
Unknown JSON properties: by default Jackson throws exception; configure with @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown=true)
ObjectMapper bean: customize globally in @Configuration class

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Spring Boot auto-configures Jackson ObjectMapper. When a @RestController method returns a Java object, Jackson serializes it to JSON automatically. When a request comes in with @RequestBody, Jackson deserializes the JSON. I use annotations to customize behavior: @JsonProperty for different key names, @JsonIgnore for sensitive fields like passwords, and @JsonFormat for date patterns. One gotcha: if the incoming JSON has extra fields Jackson doesn't recognize, it throws an exception by default — I configure Jackson to ignore unknown properties globally using ObjectMapper configuration or @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true).

seo.metaTitle: Jackson JSON Serialization Spring Boot | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn how Jackson serializes JSON in Spring Boot with annotations. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot wires Jackson in automatically — you write Java, it handles the JSON. But knowing the annotations lets you control exactly what goes in and out.

beats.text: Jackson is the JSON library Spring Boot auto-configures. When a @RestController method returns a Java object, an ObjectMapper serializes it to JSON for the response. When a request arrives with a JSON body, @RequestBody tells Jackson to deserialize it to the Java type you declared.

Without Jackson auto-configuration you'd have to manually call objectMapper.writeValueAsString(object) in every controller method and parse responses yourself. Spring Boot eliminates that so you never touch JSON strings directly.

items: @JsonProperty("user_name"): map Java field userName to JSON key user_name
@JsonIgnore: exclude a field from both serialization and deserialization — great for passwords
@JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd"): control how LocalDate or LocalDateTime is formatted
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL): skip null fields so the JSON response isn't cluttered with nulls
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true): silently skip extra JSON fields the Java class doesn't have

beats.text: Todo entity has a field lastUpdatedAt as LocalDateTime. Without configuration, Jackson produces an array of date-part numbers. Add @JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss") and it becomes a readable string. The User entity has a passwordHash field — annotate it @JsonIgnore and it never appears in GET /users responses. In Spring Boot 3 you can also configure the global ObjectMapper in a @Configuration class: objectMapper.setSerializationInclusion(NON_NULL) applies to every response. sharp edge: by default Jackson throws UnrecognizedPropertyException if the incoming JSON has a field your DTO doesn't have. Add @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) on the class or configure globally — especially important for external API responses that may add new fields.

items: Forgetting @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true) — any unexpected field in incoming JSON throws an exception and returns 400
Using @JsonIgnore on an entity field instead of using a DTO — fine for quick fixes, but a proper DTO layer is the right answer

speakable_v2.cap: Jackson = Spring Boot's auto-wired JSON engine. @JsonProperty renames, @JsonIgnore hides, @JsonFormat patterns dates, @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown) survives new API fields.

question: What is the difference between JSON serialization and deserialization?
title: JSON Serialization vs Deserialization
direct_answer: Serialization converts a Java object to JSON string (for sending in responses). Deserialization converts a JSON string back to a Java object (for processing incoming requests). In Spring Boot, Jackson handles both automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Clear understanding of the data conversion pipeline in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the direction or not knowing what triggers each
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention custom serializers/deserializers for complex types

sections.title: Serialization Direction
sections.content: Think of it as: Serialization = Java → JSON (writing). Deserialization = JSON → Java (reading). When your REST API sends data to a client, it serializes. When it receives data from a client, it deserializes. Spring Boot does this invisibly — you work with Java objects, Spring handles the conversion.

sections.title: When Each Happens
content: Serialization: return User user from @GetMapping → Jackson converts to JSON response
Deserialization: @RequestBody UserRequest request → Jackson converts JSON body to UserRequest
Custom serializer: implement JsonSerializer<T> for complex types (e.g., Money, LocalDate)
Custom deserializer: implement JsonDeserializer<T> for custom parsing
@JsonComponent — registers custom serializer/deserializer as Spring bean
Serialization excludes @JsonIgnore fields, transient fields by default

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Serialization is converting Java objects to JSON — outbound data. Deserialization is converting JSON back to Java objects — inbound data. In Spring Boot's request/response cycle: deserialization happens when a POST request body arrives and @RequestBody maps JSON to your DTO. Serialization happens when your method returns a Java object and @RestController converts it to the JSON response. If I have a custom type like Money or a weird date format, I write a custom serializer implementing JsonSerializer and register it with @JsonComponent.

seo.metaDescription: Understand serialization and deserialization in Spring Boot Jackson. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Serialization goes out, deserialization comes in — get the direction right and you'll never confuse the two again.

groups.label: Serialization
groups.text: Converting a Java object to a JSON string. This happens when your REST endpoint sends a response — your Java TodoResponse object becomes the JSON bytes the client reads.

groups.label: Deserialization
groups.text: Converting a JSON string back into a Java object. This happens when a client sends a JSON request body — the bytes become your Java CreateTodoRequest object.

items: Serialization control: @JsonIgnore hides fields, @JsonFormat formats dates, @JsonProperty renames fields in the JSON output
Deserialization control: @JsonIgnoreProperties ignores extra fields, @JsonCreator with @JsonProperty maps constructor parameters

beats.text: Todo app: client sends POST /todos with {title: Buy milk, done: false}. Jackson deserializes it to CreateTodoRequest(title=Buy milk, done=false). Service creates it. Controller returns the saved TodoResponse(id=42, title=Buy milk, done=false, createdAt=2026-06-01T...). Jackson serializes that to the JSON response. Spring Boot does both sides automatically. non-obvious: the direction matters for annotations. @JsonIgnore prevents a field from appearing in either direction. If you want a field to be write-only (accept in request but not return in response), use @JsonProperty with access = WRITE_ONLY.

speakable_v2.cap: Serialize = Java to JSON (outbound response). Deserialize = JSON to Java (inbound request). Spring Boot handles both; annotations let you control what crosses the boundary.

question: How do you validate JSON request bodies in Spring Boot?
title: Request Body Validation in Spring Boot
direct_answer: Use Bean Validation (JSR-380) annotations like @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Email on DTO fields, and add @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter. Spring automatically validates and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException on failure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of input validation — critical for API security and data integrity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Validating in service layer only, or not returning field-level error details
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show that you handle MethodArgumentNotValidException with @ControllerAdvice to return structured errors

sections.title: Bean Validation with @Valid
sections.content: Spring Boot integrates with Jakarta Bean Validation (Hibernate Validator). You annotate your DTO fields with constraints, add @Valid to @RequestBody, and Spring validates automatically before the method executes. No manual validation code needed.

sections.title: Common Validation Annotations
content: @NotNull — field must not be null
@NotBlank — string must not be null or blank
@Size(min=2, max=50) — string/collection size constraint
@Email — valid email format
@Min(0) @Max(150) — numeric range
@Pattern(regexp = "...") — custom regex
@Valid on method parameter triggers validation
MethodArgumentNotValidException → @ControllerAdvice → return 400/422 with field errors

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: I validate request bodies using Bean Validation annotations on the DTO class — @NotBlank for required strings, @Email for email fields, @Size for length constraints. Then I add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter in the controller. If validation fails, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException before my code even runs. I handle that exception in @ControllerAdvice and return a 422 response with a list of field errors — field name, rejected value, and message. This gives the client specific feedback about what's wrong.

followup_questions: What is the difference between @Valid and @Validated?
How do you create custom validation annotations?
How do you validate nested objects?

seo.metaTitle: Spring Boot Request Body Validation @Valid | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn Bean Validation with @Valid @NotNull @Email in Spring Boot. Java fresher interview prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Never trust data that arrives over the network — @Valid plus Bean Validation annotations are how you reject bad input before it reaches your service layer.

beats.text: Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation, formerly JSR-380) is a standard for declaring constraints on Java fields using annotations. You put constraint annotations on your DTO class and add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter. Spring validates the incoming JSON before your method body runs.

Without validation at the API layer, invalid data reaches your service and database. A missing required field or a negative age could cause a cryptic NullPointerException deep inside your code rather than a clean 400 or 422 response with a helpful message.

items: @NotNull: field must not be null
@NotBlank: string must not be null, empty, or whitespace
@Size(min=2, max=100): string or collection length bounds
@Email: valid email format
@Min(0) @Max(150): numeric range
@Pattern(regexp = "..."): custom regex for things like phone numbers
@Valid on @RequestBody parameter triggers validation; missing it means constraints are silently ignored

beats.text: CreateTodoRequest DTO: title field with @NotBlank and @Size(max=200), dueDate with @Future. Controller: @PostMapping with @Valid @RequestBody CreateTodoRequest request. If title is blank, Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException before entering the method. In @ControllerAdvice, catch MethodArgumentNotValidException, collect bindingResult.getFieldErrors(), and return 422 with [{field:title, message:must not be blank}]. The client gets specific, actionable feedback. production trap: forgetting @Valid on the controller parameter. The annotations on the DTO class do nothing without @Valid on the parameter — Spring won't run validation without it.

items: Forgetting @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter — constraint annotations on the DTO class are silently ignored without it
Validating only in the service layer — the service shouldn't need to handle raw invalid data; validate at the boundary

speakable_v2.cap: @NotBlank/@Size/@Email on DTO + @Valid on @RequestBody = automatic validation. Catch MethodArgumentNotValidException in @ControllerAdvice and return field-level 422 errors.

question: What is the difference between a DTO and an entity in Spring Boot JSON handling?
title: DTO vs Entity in REST APIs
direct_answer: An Entity maps to a database table and is managed by JPA. A DTO (Data Transfer Object) is a plain Java class used to send/receive data over the API. Using separate DTOs prevents over-exposing database structure and avoids serialization issues with JPA lazy loading.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architecture awareness — separating persistence layer from API layer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning @Entity objects directly from controllers — exposes internal structure, causes LazyInitializationException
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MapStruct for automatic DTO mapping and the potential for JSON infinite recursion with bidirectional JPA relationships

sections.title: Why Not Return Entities Directly?
sections.content: Returning JPA entities from REST controllers is an anti-pattern. Entities expose your database schema. Bidirectional relationships cause infinite recursion during JSON serialization (User has Orders, Order has User...). Lazy-loaded collections throw LazyInitializationException outside transaction. DTOs solve all of this.

sections.title: DTO Best Practices
content: Request DTO: what the client sends (CreateUserRequest, UpdateUserRequest)
Response DTO: what the client receives (UserResponse, UserSummary)
Entity: JPA-managed, matches database schema — stays in service/repository layer
Conversion: map Entity ↔ DTO in service layer using manual mapping or MapStruct
MapStruct: annotation processor that generates type-safe mapping code at compile time
Avoid @JsonIgnore on Entity fields — use proper DTOs instead
Use Java Records for DTOs (Java 16+): immutable, no boilerplate

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: I always use separate DTOs instead of returning entities directly. Returning entities causes several problems: it exposes your database schema, bidirectional JPA relationships cause infinite JSON serialization loops, and lazy-loaded collections throw exceptions when Jackson tries to serialize them outside a transaction. My pattern is: controller receives a RequestDTO, service converts it to an Entity for database work, then converts back to a ResponseDTO for the return value. For mapping, I use MapStruct which generates the conversion code at compile time. Java Records are great for DTOs because they're immutable and have no boilerplate.

seo.metaTitle: DTO vs Entity in Spring Boot REST APIs | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn why to use DTOs instead of entities in REST APIs. MapStruct, JSON serialization. Fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Always use DTOs in your REST layer — returning JPA entities directly is an anti-pattern with real production consequences.

groups.label: Entity
groups.text: A JPA-managed class that maps to a database table. It lives in the persistence layer, carries JPA annotations like @Id and @OneToMany, and may have lazy-loaded collections.

groups.label: DTO (Data Transfer Object)
groups.text: A plain Java class (or record) designed purely for API data exchange. It has no JPA annotations, contains only what the client needs to see or send, and can be validated with Bean Validation.

items: Always use a DTO at the controller layer — never return an @Entity directly from @RestController
Use separate request DTOs (CreateTodoRequest) and response DTOs (TodoResponse) to control exactly what comes in and what goes out

beats.text: Todo entity has a User owner with @ManyToOne and User has a List of Todos with @OneToMany — bidirectional. Return the entity from @GetMapping and Jackson serializes Todo, then User, then User's todos, then each todo's user, then... stack overflow. The fix: a TodoResponse DTO with just {id, title, done, ownerName} — no JPA relationships, no recursion. Conversion from Entity to DTO is done in the service layer using manual mapping or MapStruct, which generates the code at compile time. production trap: @JsonIgnore on entity fields is a band-aid, not a fix. It couples your JPA model to your API contract. Use proper DTOs.

speakable_v2.cap: Entity = database concern. DTO = API concern. Never mix them. Return DTOs from controllers. Map Entity to DTO in the service layer. Use MapStruct for zero-boilerplate mapping.
